youtube_description:
⚡ Solar keeps climbing while coal keeps slipping—watch the market “power shift” unfold year-by-year.

CHAPTERS
00:00 — The coal era still looks unbreakable
01:10 — Solar costs fall; orders accelerate
02:30 — 2015–2018: the supply chain ramps fast
03:55 — 2019–2021: policy + plummeting module prices
05:10 — 2022: energy stress pushes clean buildout
06:30 — 2023–2025: coal economics tighten further
07:40 — 2026 estimate: solar outscales coal

WHAT YOU’RE WATCHING
This chart-race uses global industry revenue estimates as a proxy for investment and market pull:
• Solar PV supply-chain revenue rises from ~$80B (2010) to ~$1.78T (2026 est.)
• Coal-fired power industry revenue falls from ~$820B (2010) to ~$665B (2026 est.)
• Wind strengthens the clean-power trend as a second growth lane
• Oil & gas acts like the competing “capital magnet,” spiking during shocks

WHY IT MATTERS
Solar didn’t just grow—it grew faster than incumbents could adjust. Meanwhile, coal faced a perfect storm: slower demand growth, tighter carbon/air rules, and renewables winning new capacity additions.

If you want more high-contrast chart races like this, hit LIKE, SUBSCRIBE, and comment the rival matchup you want next.

instagram_caption:
🚀 Solar just outpaced coal so hard the entire electricity story flipped.

In 2010, the world’s clean buildout was still tiny compared to coal. Solar’s global supply-chain revenue sat around **$80B**, while coal-fired power was a behemoth at about **$820B**. For a while, it looked like coal would remain the default “default power,” because it was already built, already financed, and already everywhere.

Then the inflection hit. Between **2012–2015**, solar climbed from roughly **$110B → $190B** as module costs fell and manufacturing scale-up accelerated. By **2016**, solar crossed **$235B**, and the momentum stacked: **$360B (2018)**, **$460B (2019)**. Coal, meanwhile, slowly bled out—**$805B (2018)** and **$790B (2019)**—not crashing overnight, but losing the new-growth contest.

The real punch comes after the energy shocks. In **2021**, solar surged to about **$720B** while coal dipped to **$760B**. In **2022**, renewables grabbed attention globally as energy volatility made new clean capacity more attractive: solar jumped to **~$980B**, while coal slipped to **~$740B**. By **2023**, coal sat near **$720B** and solar reached **~$1.15T**—a gap that’s no longer just a trend, it’s a re-ordering.

And the “chart-race ending” is dramatic: by **2025**, solar is around **$1.62T** while coal is about **$685B**. The 2026 estimate pushes solar to **$1.78T** and coal to **$665B**—meaning solar is now roughly **2.7×** the coal industry market size by this proxy.

🔥 Question for you: Do you think the next bottleneck is **grid buildout** or **permitting**—and which country/region will move first?
facebook_caption:
Solar versus coal captures the core of the global energy transition: renewables scaled rapidly while coal’s economic and policy headwinds tightened. In this timeline comparison (global industry revenue proxy), solar PV supply-chain revenue rises from about $80B in 2010 to roughly $1.62T in 2025, reaching an estimated ~$1.78T in 2026. Over the same period, coal-fired power industry revenue declines from about $820B to approximately $685B by 2025, with an estimated ~$665B in 2026.

The inflection accelerates after mid-decade cost declines and then intensifies during the post-2021 energy volatility, where solar climbs sharply from ~$720B (2021) to ~$980B (2022). Coal declines more gradually, but the gap widens each year as clean capacity additions outcompete new coal build and coal’s relative economics deteriorate.

Watch how wind also strengthens the broader clean-power trajectory, while oil & gas spikes show how capital migrates during energy shocks.
